title: The Way of the Saviour
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino del Salvador
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The Camino del Salvador is a short road with a mountain in the middle of it. It leaves León, follows the Bernesga river north, crosses the Cantabrian range, and drops through the mining valleys of Asturias to Oviedo: ~120 km by the CaminoPlus catalog. It ends at the cathedral of San Salvador, the Saviour, and not at Santiago.
The promise of this book is simple.

By the last page you will know why pilgrims have taken this detour since the Middle Ages, what the one hard day asks of you, how the days can be cut, what the certificate of Oviedo is, and what the Pilgrim's Office says about a walk that does not end in Santiago.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the six walking days, and the chapter on other ways to split them, which matters here because the sources count five days, six or nine. Read the safety chapter before you go, not after.
If you are on the road tonight, go to your stage. If you are only dreaming, read "Is this Camino for you?" and "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change, and in the mountains a wrong guess costs more than anywhere. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
It is also
not a Compostela book

. The Compostela is the certificate of the Pilgrim's Office for a walk that arrives at the cathedral of Santiago, and this walk arrives at Oviedo. The chapter on arriving says what the Office says, and what Oviedo's cathedral offers instead.
Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate and the published figures differ. Where something depends on the day (snow, fog, a swollen stream), the book says
check before you go
, and means it. On this road the line matters most on the third day.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a card stamped along the way; each stamp is a
sello
. The
Salvadorana
is the certificate that Oviedo's cathedral gives to those who have walked this road. A
puerto
is a mountain pass.
The official pages in Asturias give place names in Spanish and in Asturian (Oviedo and Uviéu, Pajares and Payares). This book uses the Spanish forms.
Carry what the mountain asks for, and take the short day slowly.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Camino del Salvador starts in León, "at the gates of the old pilgrims' hospital of San Marcos", in the words of Turismo Asturias, the tourism service of the Principado de Asturias. The Junta de Castilla y León's guide says San Marcos is where the Camino Francés and the Camino del Salvador part. The road ends at the cathedral of San Salvador in Oviedo.

The Confraternity of St James describes the shape of it. The first ~40 km, as far as Buiza, follow the valley of the Bernesga and are fairly flat, on paths and very minor roads. The next ~25 km cross the Cordillera to the village of Pajares, in Asturias, with two quite substantial climbs and descents. After that the road falls through the valleys of the Lena and the Caudal to Oviedo. Asturias calls this the mining basin. The Junta's guide names Arbás del Puerto as the last place in Castilla y León.
How long

The CaminoPlus catalog gives ~120 km, and so does the Confraternity. The Junta's guide, updated in 2011, counts ~120.3 km, of which ~58.8 are in Castilla y León. Asturias gives no total. It publishes its part as three stages that add up to ~59.5 km (~22.1, ~19.0 and ~18.4), counted from the pass, where the Junta's guide counts ~61.5 km from Arbás.

Others differ. The cathedral of Oviedo says ~122 km, though its own six stage figures add up to ~120.3. The association of the municipalities on the León side gives ~121 km in one place and ~123 in another. The Junta's leaflet map runs to ~125 km, and Spanish Wikipedia says ~116. The gaps come from where a source starts counting and which line it follows. This book uses ~120 km.
The catalog calls the road the Camino del Salvador. Asturias writes Camino de El Salvador, and the cathedral and the Junta also use Camino de San Salvador.
Salvador
means Saviour, and the cathedral at the end is dedicated to him.
The usual six days
Oviedo's cathedral and the association of the León municipalities both divide the road into six stages with the same stage towns, and this book follows them, with the cathedral's figures:

items.t: León to La Robla: ~27 km.
La Robla to Poladura de la Tercia: ~23 km.
Poladura de la Tercia to Pajares: ~14 km.
Pajares to Pola de Lena: ~24 km.
Pola de Lena to Mieres: ~13 km.
Mieres to Oviedo: ~19 km.

spans.t: The third day is the short one, and the mountain day. Other counts exist, and the chapter on other ways to split the days sets them out.
Why it exists

Oviedo's cathedral keeps the Cámara Santa, the Holy Chamber, and in it an ark of relics. The cathedral's page tells the older story as tradition: the ark left Jerusalem when the Persians took it in 614, travelled through North Africa and Spain, was hidden on a mountain near Oviedo, and was brought into the city under King Alfonso II. What is documented begins on 13 March 1075, when King Alfonso VI, passing through Oviedo on his own pilgrimage to Santiago, saw the ark opened before bishops and the court. The record of that day lists many relics. The one that stands out is the
sudarium
, the linen cloth that covered Christ's head after his death.

Asturias says the discovery made Oviedo a centre of pilgrimage in its own right. The Junta's guide says that by the end of the eleventh century the basilica had become the second pilgrimage centre of the medieval peninsula. The Confraternity says the purpose of the walk is to visit the Sudarium, and points to the Gospel of John, chapter 20, verses 6 and 7.
A saying carried the idea. Asturias gives it as a popular verse that people still recite:
Quien va a Santiago y no al Salvador, visita al criado y olvida al Señor.
Whoever goes to Santiago and not to the Saviour visits the servant and forgets the Lord. The Junta writes
deja
, "leaves", for the last verb, and the sources differ on the origin: Asturias calls it medieval and popular, the cathedral and the Confraternity call it French. This book does not choose.
A detour, not a road to Santiago

Asturias says the road began as a detour from the Camino Francés, one that let those who took it join the Camino Primitivo if they wished, and also gave the walk a meaningful end in its own right. The cathedral says that for many pilgrims it was the end of the journey, and for many others the start of the road to Santiago. Spanish Wikipedia adds that from Oviedo they could go on by the coastal road or by the Primitivo. Asturias says that quite a few took the road home from Compostela, to kneel before the Lord they had passed on the way out.
Why it faded, and why it is back

The Junta's guide gives three reasons for the decline. Legends told of the hardness and danger of the road. A new main road, today's N-630, was opened in the eighteenth century. And the confiscations of church property in the nineteenth century, with the loss of convents and hospitals, left the route almost forgotten. The same guide, in 2011, says it is increasingly used by pilgrims. Today the Salvador has its own credencial and its own certificate, and the chapter on arriving explains both.
Short, and not easy

The CaminoPlus catalog rates the Camino del Salvador 4 on a scale of 1 to 5. The Primitivo and the Norte get a 4 as well, the Francés a 3, and the Inglés a 2. The distance is small, so the rating is about the mountain.

The sources agree on that, in different tones. Asturias calls the road essentially a mountain route, and says the Asturian side is not to be underestimated either, even with the pass behind you. The association of the León municipalities says the road is not exceptionally difficult, but that parts of it cross high mountain, with big changes of height and a top of more than ~1,500 m, and that some preparation is wise. The Confraternity of St James says the mountain terrain brings poor weather, and services so scant that careful planning of where to stay and eat matters. It reports a stretch of ~50 km with no shops.
Who it suits

items.t: You have five or six days, or up to nine if you want to go gently.
You are happy to walk all day on mountain tracks, to read a forecast, and to change the plan when the forecast says so.
You want a walk with a destination that matters in itself: the cathedral of Oviedo and its Holy Chamber.
You want to begin the Camino Primitivo at its source with a few days of preparation behind you.
You can carry food and water for a day, and you have a plan B.

spans.t: Whatever brings you, the road asks the same of you: to be ready for the weather.
Who might choose another road

items.t: If you need a shop, a cafe and a bed in every village. The mountain days will not give you that.
If you can only walk in the snowy months. The association says plainly not to venture onto the mountain when it is snowed over.
If you want a Compostela from this walk alone. It ends at Oviedo, and the chapter on arriving explains what that means.
If your knees dislike steep descents. Asturias praises the scenery as you come down from the pass, and the association says the descents of the fourth day are what will test your knees.
If you want company. No source read for this book gives a count of pilgrims on this road, so ask locally.

spans.t: How it compares with its neighbours

The Camino Francés leaves León to the west. The Salvador turns north into the range. The Camino Primitivo, which begins where this road ends, is ~320 km and mountainous too, and has its own book in this series,
The Original Way
. The Salvador is the short one: a few days, with a high pass and a goal.
You do not have to walk all of it

Asturias publishes its part of the road as three stages, ~59.5 km in all, counted from the pass. The association says the hostels allow up to nine days, and that in bad weather the mountain stages can be left for another time, by taxi, train or bus. Oviedo's cathedral gives the Salvadorana to those who show a stamped credencial, with one stamp per stage enough, and its page names no minimum distance. If you plan to walk only part of the road and want the certificate, ask the cathedral first.
The mountain makes its own weather

The Confraternity of St James says it plainly. In León province July and August are very hot, much as on the Camino Francés. The weather on the crossing of the Cordillera is highly variable, with thick fog, heavy rain and severe cold all possible, and the Asturian side can be very different from the León side on the same day. Spanish Wikipedia describes the Puerto de Pajares, the road pass over the range, as known for its winter snowfalls and for fog on summer nights.

The numbers below are for the two cities at the ends, and neither is the mountain. Wikipedia gives them from the Spanish state weather agency, AEMET, for 1991 to 2020. León's station stands at ~916 m, Oviedo's at ~336 m, and the walk climbs from ~837 m at León to a high point of ~1,568 m. Expect the crossing to be colder and wetter than either table.

items.t: León, winter.
The January average high is ~7 °C and the average low ~−1 °C. The lowest temperature on record is ~−17 °C.
León, summer.
The July average high is ~27 °C, and the record is ~38 °C. July is the driest month (~18 mm of rain), in a year of ~496 mm.
Oviedo, winter.
The January average high is ~12 °C and the low ~5 °C. The record low is ~−6 °C.
Oviedo, summer.
The August average high is ~24 °C, and the record ~41 °C.
Oviedo, rain.
~1,028 mm a year. July is the driest month (~44 mm) and November the wettest (~134 mm).

spans.t: León is high and dry, Oviedo green and wet. The walk passes from one to the other over the range, so you meet both.
Seasons
Winter.

The association of the León municipalities says snow often begins in December, or somewhat later, and that nobody can predict it: some winters bring hardly any, others heavy falls. Its advice is to heed what the hostel tells you, and if the hostel says conditions are bad, not to venture out, because the Way will always be there for another time.
Spring and autumn.

The association says the streams of the third day can carry a lot of water in the thaw, and that the forest of Valgrande is muddy. It recommends mountain boots in spring, in autumn and, above all, in winter.
Summer.

The association says that in summer, with good fitness, you may plan longer stages, and that the days can be very hot and the nights cool at altitude. The CaminoPlus route guide in the app, a hand-written overview and not live data, suggests June to September. No source read for this book names a best month, so treat that as a suggestion.
Daylight

These are the book's own figures, calculated from a standard solar formula for León, in local clock time. They are approximate, so check them against a sun table before you plan. Mountain valleys lose the sun sooner than open ground.

items.t: Late December: sunrise ~08:50, sunset ~17:50, ~9 hours of daylight.
Early November: sunset ~18:10, ~10 hours.
Late March: sunrise ~07:30, sunset ~19:35, ~12 hours.
Late June: sunrise ~06:45, sunset ~22:05, ~15 hours.
Late September: sunset ~20:20, ~12 hours.

spans.t: In late autumn and winter, the association says, leave a margin of daylight for the unexpected.
Crowds, and checking

No source read for this book gives a count of pilgrims on this road, and the Pilgrim's Office's statistics page could not be read. Whether a hostel is open in your month is a question for the app and for a call, not for this book.
Check before you go.

Snow, fog, a swollen stream, a diverted path: they change from year to year and from day to day. AEMET publishes warnings and town forecasts, in English as well as Spanish. Read the forecast for the villages you will cross, remember that it understates the ridge above them, and ask the hostel the evening before.
Your credencial

The credencial is your pilgrim's passport, stamped at the end of each day. It gets you into the pilgrims' hostels, Asturias and the association both say, and you show it in Oviedo to ask for the Salvadorana.

A credencial made for this road exists. The Confraternity of St James says it is available from the cathedral in León, and the association of the León municipalities names the tourist offices of La Robla and La Pola de Gordón, the seat in León of the pilgrim association, and hostels along the way. You do not need it. Oviedo's cathedral says that any other model is valid, and the association says the same of the official pilgrim credencial. Churches, hostels and tourist offices keep stamps, says Asturias, and Oviedo's cathedral will stamp the credencial of any pilgrim who asks, whatever Camino they walk.
For the Salvadorana the cathedral asks for a credencial stamped at the places you pass, and says one stamp per stage will do.
Getting to León, and home from Oviedo

Wikipedia says León has a long-distance railway station, with high-speed services to Madrid in about two hours and direct trains to Galicia, Asturias and Valladolid. León's airport is ~6 km from the centre and flies mostly within Spain. Oviedo has a railway station with long-distance, regional and suburban services, and Asturias Airport lies ~48 km from the city, linked to it by motorway and a scheduled bus. Look up times on the operators' own pages.

Under the pass, high-speed trains now run in a tunnel of ~24.7 km, part of the line between León and Gijón, which Wikipedia says opened to passengers on 30 November 2023. You will cross the same range over the top, on foot.
Training, boots and the pack

Asturias advises starting to walk a few months before you leave, in comfortable shoes that you have already used, and carrying sandals for the evenings. It says a rucksack should not pass ~10 kg, and that a torch and a walking stick are indispensable. Add the association's advice for this road: mountain boots in spring, autumn and above all winter.

The association's list for the pack includes a sleeping bag, a water bottle, poles, a torch, a change of clothes, good socks, a cap, plasters, a waterproof, sunscreen and sunglasses, and a first-aid kit, with your identity card, credencial, health card and a bank card or cash. It also says to forget the "just in case" items, because the road passes several important villages with the services you need. The Confraternity says that in the mountains pilgrim services are scant. They describe different stretches, so pack by the second warning and plan by both.
Food, beds and a phone call

Carry food and water for the day. The association says some villages on the first stage have no services. The Confraternity strongly recommends phoning ahead to book any accommodation that is not a pilgrims' hostel, and says that in several places you must phone ahead to be sure a meal can be bought in for you. This book gives no phone numbers, because they change.
Tell someone

Both the Confraternity and the association ask you to tell someone outside your group where and when you are walking, so that the alarm can be raised if you do not arrive when expected. Keep your phone charged, save your map on it before you leave the valley, and do not rely on signal in the mountains.
Language and waymarking
The Confraternity says a little Spanish helps, especially if you need to ask for directions on the crossing of the Cordillera.

It calls the waymarking generally very good, with a warning: in the mountains, and in bad weather above all, make sure you find and follow the signs. The association describes markers, wooden posts and yellow arrows on the ground in León province, and the usual stone markers with the scallop shell in Asturias. Its words: as long as you watch for them, it is almost impossible to leave the road.
The character of these days

The first two days follow the Bernesga river north, out of a city and into a narrowing valley. The ground is mostly streets, paths and dirt tracks, with small ups and downs that never quite let you forget you are climbing. On the second day, after Buiza, the first real mountain arrives.

The lengths in this book follow the page of Oviedo's cathedral, which gives six usual stages that add up to ~120.3 km. The association of the León municipalities gives slightly different figures, and the chapter on other ways to split the days names every source. Treat each figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
Day 1: León to La Robla (~27 km)

You start at the gates of the old pilgrims' hospital of San Marcos, where the Camino Francés and the Salvador part. The association says the first waymark stands on the pilgrims' avenue to the right of it, and that a plaque set in the ground points left for Santiago and right for the Saviour. It is a good place to stand for a minute.

The way follows the Bernesga on city streets. The association says that a signed riverside path saves you ~7 km of asphalt. Then come paths through woods of oak and holm oak to Carbajal de la Legua. The Junta de Castilla y León's guide gives it a long past: a twelfth-century foundation of Augustinian canons, replaced in 1147 by Benedictine nuns from San Pelayo in León, whom the guide says were affectionately known as
las Carbajalas
. It places the old Roman road from León to Oviedo near Cabanillas, the next village.

Near the end you pass the chapel of Celada, which the Junta says is Gothic in origin, from the fourteenth century, and altered in the seventeenth and eighteenth. Then the association's "door and hand of the pilgrim" welcome you to La Robla, which you enter under the main road and over the railway.

The association rates the day easy and warns that the ground is not flat: the constant small rises and falls will test your stamina. Carry food and water for the whole day, since the association says some villages on it offer nothing.
Day 2: La Robla to Poladura de la Tercia (~23 km)

The association divides this day in two. The first half is easy and almost flat, as far as La Pola de Gordón. After it come ~5 km of asphalt that cannot be avoided, because the road is squeezed between mountains and river as far as Buiza. The Junta's guide calls Buiza an important crossing of Roman roads, pilgrim roads and royal roads, and says it is named in 1036, in the donation of the place by King Fernando I to the cathedral of Oviedo.

At Buiza the second half begins, and with it the mountain. The association says that in ~2.5 km you reach the top of the Forcadas de San Antón, at ~1,450 m, "as spectacular as hard". The Junta's leaflet map marks ~1,462 m, and the association gives ~1,459 m on another page, so sources differ by ~10 m on a hill this size. Then you descend through a gully called the Barrancón and follow a track to San Martín and Poladura de la Tercia. The association rates the whole day medium to high.

There is an option at the Barrancón. You can stay on the track and pass through the gorges of Rodiezmo to the Cruz de la Salve. From there, the association says, pilgrims once saw the shrine of Golpejar and the chapel of Barrio, and prayed a
Salve

for protection as they looked at the mountains they would cross the next day. This way is only ~200 m longer and the two meet again ~1 km further on. The association calls it a good choice if the path through the Barrancón is under snow. At the Cruz de la Salve the way turns sharply left onto a larger track. If you miss the turn you reach Rodiezmo and must walk the rest by road.
The association's longer plans cut this day in two at Buiza. Whichever you choose, arrive in Poladura with something left: the day that follows is short and hard.
The character of this day
This is the short day and the hard one. The association calls it the
etapa reina
, the queen stage, and rates it at the top of its scale. It is the day on which the Camino del Salvador crosses the Cantabrian range, and the day on which a bad forecast should change your plan.
The heights below are as the sources give them, and the sources differ a little. Treat them as a guide to how far up you go, not as a surveyed list.

items.t: León: ~837 m (Wikipedia and the association agree).
La Robla: ~950 m (the association).
Buiza: ~1,130 m (the association).
Poladura de la Tercia: ~1,225 m (Wikipedia), ~1,230 m (the association).
Forcadas de San Antón: ~1,450 m (the association), ~1,462 m (the Junta's leaflet).
Alto de la Gobia: ~1,418 m (the Junta's leaflet).

The high point of the whole Way: ~1,568 m (the association names it as the Collada del Coito; the Junta's leaflet marks ~1,567 m and ~1,568 m, for El Cuchillo and El Canto la Tusa, on the stretch between Poladura and Arbás).

spans.t: The Puerto de Pajares itself, the road pass, is ~1,378 m, says Spanish Wikipedia. That figure is not your high point. The walking line crosses the ridge above the pass first, where the highest ground is ~190 m above the road, then comes down to Arbás and climbs again towards the pass.
Day 3: Poladura de la Tercia to Pajares (~14 km)

The association's description is short and clear. You climb steep ramps to the Cruz del Salvador, then to the Collada del Coito, the highest point of the whole Way. Ahead lies the Sierra del Cuchillo, which you cross before you drop to the collegiate church at Arbás. From the top of the Pajares pass ~5 km of descent through forest remain. The whole route runs on tracks and mountain paths. There are several streams to cross, which the association says may carry a lot of water in the thaw, and mud in the forest of Valgrande.

In snow, the association says, the snowfields on this day can make the crossing very difficult, even impossible, and the safety chapter has the rest. If the forecast is good, start early and give the day its whole length. It is only ~14 km, but it is the association's pick for the day that takes most out of you.

Arbás del Puerto is the last place in Castilla y León on the road, and it is worth the stop. Asturias says the road would be incomplete without a visit to the village and its collegiate church of Santa María, from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a milestone on the way to San Salvador in Oviedo. The Junta's guide calls the church a fine example of rural Leonese Romanesque, and says that the stories of its founding are many while the documented history is thin. What it says about the pilgrims is better than any legend. In foggy weather the bells were rung so that pilgrims would not lose their way. And pilgrims were awaited at a place called the
canto de los pobres
and walked to the hospital that stood opposite the monastery and has since gone.

From Arbás a path climbs to the Alto de la Gobia and the Boquete de La Calera, says Asturias, then drops by the valley of La Casa Tibigracias to Samiguel del Río and the village of Payares, as Asturias writes it (Pajares in Spanish), the first village in Asturias. The Junta's guide notes that in Pajares an old Calle Real still runs through the village, and that an arch and a stone house recall the pilgrims' hospital. You have crossed. Tell someone you have arrived.
The character of these days

Asturias puts it fairly. The hardest part, the climb to the pass, is behind you, but the climbs to Chanos, to El Padrún and to Picullanza and La Manxoya, it says, call for a good state of fitness. In return the road gives majestic landscapes, above all as you come down from Payares, and a singular route through the mining basin that follows the Lena and the Caudal. Green is the colour of Asturias, as the association notes, and the stone markers carry the scallop shell.

The three Asturian stages on the Turismo Asturias website, ~22.1, ~19.0 and ~18.4 km, begin at the pass and break at Campomanes and Mieres. The usual six-stage plan in this book breaks at Pola de Lena and Mieres instead, and the chapter on other ways to split the days sets them side by side.
Day 4: Pajares to Pola de Lena (~24 km)

The sources draw this day in more than one way. Asturias takes the road to Floracebos, then a path by the chapel of the Virgen de las Nieves to La Romía and down to Naveo. It climbs the Alto de Torones, descends steeply to Fierros, climbs hard to Fresneo, and comes down through woods of chestnut and holly, by the village of Erías, to Campomanes. The association describes a variant by San Miguel del Río and Llanos de Somerón, and the Junta's leaflet marks a winter line and a summer line near Pajares. Follow the markers, and ask at your hostel the night before which line is good that day.

The association says the day's difficulty is in the descents, which test your knees, and that from Campomanes the walking is completely flat. It places the day in the Natural Park of Las Ubiñas and La Mesa.

At Campomanes, the Junta's guide says, the roads over the Pajares and La Cubilla passes meet, and by the river runs the Roman road from León to Gijón. Before the day ends comes the little church of Santa Cristina de Lena. Asturias calls it one of the most paradigmatic pre-Romanesque buildings in Asturias, built in the time of the Asturian monarchy, and singles out its superb iconostasis.
Day 5: Pola de Lena to Mieres (~13 km)

The association rates this day easy and calls it a rest after the hard ramps behind you and before the ones ahead. It begins by a service road of an industrial estate. In Villallana, the association says, the church of San Martín stands beside the
Hospitalón
, a former pilgrims' hospital. In Ujo, Asturias says, the church of Santa Eulalia keeps a Romanesque doorway and apse.

There is one warning. The association says that the official markers from Pola de Lena to Ujo follow the old national road, and calls that completely inadvisable for its danger. It suggests following the yellow arrows of a recently recovered stretch that avoids the asphalt. Check the current line before you go, and walk the one that keeps you off the road.

Asturias advises the riverside path along the Caudal from Ujo to Mieres, crossing by the Ponte Verde, where the traditional crossing was. The town's name carries the road in it: Asturias says Mieres del Camín, still often called "del Camino", is one of the traces left by the Jacobean tradition in Asturian place names. You enter by the bridge of La Perra and leave by the Plaza del Requejo, one of the squares Asturias calls the incomparable cathedral of Asturian cider.
Day 6: Mieres to Oviedo (~19 km)

The association calls it a clearly urban stage, with asphalt for much of it, some good stretches that avoid it, and a stretch on a Roman road. It rises and falls all the way, with El Padrún, La Manzaneda and La Manxoya as the short climbs, and it is short enough to be comfortable.

Asturias names the places. At La Rebollá there was once an inn, and the parish church keeps a few Romanesque corbels. On the way into Olloniego you cross a footbridge over the dual carriageway and the railway, and Asturias singles out the town's Romanesque bridge and its keep and castle. Then you climb by the base of the peak of Arnea and cross the valley of the Gafo to La Manxoya.
From La Manxoya, Asturias says, it is told that the old pilgrims cried out
¡Mi Dios!
, an exclamation of awe, when they saw the tower of the cathedral on the horizon. The walk ends by the district of San Lázaro and the cathedral of San Salvador with its Holy Chamber.

chapters.title: Other ways to split the days

spans.t: What the sources count

There is no single agreed list of stages. Asturias says the official route recognises five stages, the last three in Asturias, and publishes those three (~22.1, ~19.0 and ~18.4 km). It does not name the first two. Oviedo's cathedral and the association of the León municipalities both give the six stages of the first chapter, and this book follows them, but their figures differ a little. The association's front page says ~24 km for the second day, ~25 for the fourth, ~14 for the fifth and ~19 for the sixth, which Asturias counts as ~18. One page of the association gives ~14 km for the fourth day. That is the third day's figure and no other source agrees, so this book does not use it. The cathedral's six figures add up to ~120.3 km, though its text says ~122.
Gentler plans

The association also suggests plans of five, seven, eight and nine days. They are rough: its own pages give ~24.8 km for Bendueños to Mieres in one plan and ~16.8 km in another. Its nine-day plan, the gentlest, runs:

items.t: León to Cabanillas: ~17.5 km.
Cabanillas to La Robla: ~9.5 km.
La Robla to Buiza: ~13.5 km.
Buiza to Poladura de la Tercia: ~9.7 km.
Poladura de la Tercia to Pajares: ~14.1 km.
Pajares to Bendueños: ~16.8 km.
Bendueños to Pola de Lena: ~10.7 km.
Pola de Lena to Mieres: ~14.1 km.
Mieres to Oviedo: ~19 km.

spans.t: These add up to ~125 km, a little more than the six-day route. The plan cuts the second day at Buiza, so the climb to the Forcadas de San Antón falls on a short day, and it spreads the long fourth day over three shorter ones. In its shorter plans the association offers other ends for the mountain days: Poladura to Llanos de Somerón (~18.7 km) or to Bendueños instead of Poladura to Pajares. Its five-day plan joins Pola de Lena to Oviedo in one day, ~32 km by the figures above, a long day.
Two lines between Buiza and Arbás

The line that the association, the cathedral and the Junta's leaflet draw climbs by the Forcadas de San Antón and Poladura de la Tercia. The Junta's guide gives ~9.5 km from Buiza to Poladura and ~9 km on to Arbás, ~18.5 km in all.

The same guide says the route it describes goes another way: down the valley by Villasimpliz, Villamanín, Villanueva de la Tercia and Busdongo to Arbás. Its table adds up to ~18.7 km for that line, about the same. Spanish Wikipedia calls the valley line the main route and the Poladura line an alternative. The Confraternity of St James mentions an unofficial, unsigned winter route, an escape from the mountains in bad weather, described in its own guidebook. Whether that is the valley line this book cannot say.

The association, for its part, says the road is never an alternative. These accounts pull in different directions, so before the second night ask your host which lines are waymarked and passable that week.
Taking only part of it

Asturias's three stages cover ~59.5 km from the pass, so a walk of a few days starts there, and you would need to reach the pass yourself. In bad weather the association's advice is a taxi, a train or a bus past the mountain, and a return another time. The cathedral's page names no minimum distance for the Salvadorana, so ask before you plan on it.
The pilgrims' hostels

Asturias says the stages of the Camino de Santiago begin and end in towns with hostels, public or private, and that the roads through Asturias have enough places to sleep for every pilgrim. The Confraternity of St James says there are albergues and other suitable accommodation on this road, and the association says there is enough infrastructure to do it in as many as nine days. This book does not say which village has what. That changes, and the app and the hostels' own pages have the current answer.
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: shared rooms, bunks, a
hospitalero

(the host) who checks your credencial and stamps it. Bring a sleeping bag, which the association's own list includes. Keep your pack off the bed and your boots by the door, and pack the night before so that you are not rustling at five in the morning. Everyone else walks tomorrow too.

Some hostels in the mountain villages are small, as the Junta's leaflet map shows. The Confraternity strongly recommends phoning ahead to book any accommodation that is not a pilgrims' hostel, and it says that in some places a meal must be arranged by phone beforehand so that the food can be bought in. Do that before the long days. The tourist offices and the hostels' pages have the numbers; this book gives none.
Eating
Eat when you can, and carry food and water for the day. The Confraternity warns of a stretch of ~50 km without shops, and the association says some villages on the first day offer no services.
When you do sit down, the Junta's guide has a good deal to say about the table of the valleys of Gordón and La Tercia: cured meats and sausages (
chorizo
, ham,
botillos
longaniza
morcilla
), lentils, beans and cabbage, game and trout, and a dish called
entrecogido
, a platter built on the meats of the
matanza
, the traditional pig-killing. Do not count on all of it. Ask what the kitchen has.
Resting

The association's advice about pace is as plain as its advice about snow: do not run, rest as much as you need, and you will find the stages comfortable. The third day is short in kilometres and long in effort, so plan an early night after it. Both ends of the road are cities worth a day: León before you start, and Oviedo, where the cathedral and its Holy Chamber are the reason you came.

A taxi is a tool, not a failure. The association notes that taxis are much used on this road, for tired legs, for a short cut to a shop or a bed, and for a day when the mountain says no. Use one without apology.
This chapter is plain on purpose. Nothing here is a reason to be afraid of this road. It is a list of the things worth taking seriously on a short one with a mountain in it.
Feet and legs

Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it before it becomes a blister, keep your feet clean and dry, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty. The association says the difficulty of the fourth day is the descents, which will test your knees, so take the steep ground slowly and use poles if you carry them. If a knee, a shin or the top of a foot gives you a sharp or growing pain, stop. A day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury. For anything that worries you, see a doctor or a pharmacist.
The third day
This is the one day where a forecast should decide what you do.

items.t: Fog.

The Confraternity says the crossing may bring thick fog. Waymarking is generally very good, it adds, but in the mountains and in bad weather you must make sure you find the signs and follow them. If you cannot see the next marker, stop and wait, or go back to the last one.
Rain and cold.

The Confraternity lists heavy rain and severe cold, and the association says nights at altitude are cool even in summer. Carry a waterproof, a warm layer and a hat, and keep one dry set of clothes in a bag that cannot get wet.
Water and snow.

In the thaw, the association says, the streams on this day can carry a lot of water, so do not cross one you cannot see the bottom of. The snowfields can make the crossing very difficult, even impossible. Its rule is to avoid the mountain when it is snowed over, to listen to the hostel when it says conditions are bad, and to leave the stage for another time. The Way, it says, will always be there.
Time.
Start early, with daylight in hand. Anyone can twist an ankle, and in the mountains with few hours of light that is a serious problem, as the association puts it.

spans.t: The road is not an escape

The association is blunt: the road is never an alternative. In snow, it says, the ploughs clear the carriageway first and not the verge, and it calls the road one of the most dangerous in Spain. Its advice is a taxi, a train or a bus, and the mountain stages left for another day.

The Confraternity mentions an unofficial, unsigned winter route, kept in its own guidebook, as an escape from the mountains in bad weather. This book has no details of it, and no source read says how the two pieces of advice fit together. Ask at the hostel the evening before what is passable that week.
Other roads, other days

items.t: The second day
has ~5 km of asphalt between the river and the mountainside, the association says, which cannot be avoided.
The fifth day.

The association says the official markers from Pola de Lena to Ujo follow the old national road, and calls that completely inadvisable for its danger. It points to yellow arrows on a recovered stretch that avoids the road. Check the current line before you go.
On any road,
face the oncoming traffic, keep to the edge and wear something bright. Never walk on a road in the dark.
In July and August,
the Confraternity says, León province is very hot. The first two days are in the valley, and a hot day there is a long one. Start early and carry more water than seems sensible.

spans.t: When to stop

Tell someone where you will sleep each night, and message them when you arrive. Keep your phone charged and your map saved on it, and do not rely on signal in the mountains. If you are tired, ill or frightened by the weather, stop. The road will be there tomorrow.
AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency, publishes warnings and town forecasts. Read them the night before and again at breakfast.
In an emergency in Spain, call 112,

the European emergency number. Your Europe, the EU's information service, says it works in every EU country alongside the national numbers, that callers are answered in the language or languages of the country, and that English is offered in some countries only. Do not count on it. Know the Spanish name of the last village you passed, and say where you are as exactly as you can.

People walk this road for many reasons, and they do not have to be yours. Some walk out of faith. The road ends at the Holy Chamber of Oviedo, where, the cathedral says, the most venerated relic is the
sudarium

, kept there since the ninth century. Some walk to find their legs before the Camino Primitivo. Some walk for sport, or for a rest from work, or because a mountain is a good place to be quiet. Some walk out of grief, at a turning point, or from curiosity about what is on the other side of the range. All are welcome on the road, and none needs to defend the reason.
A detour on purpose
Quien va a Santiago y no al Salvador, visita al criado y olvida al Señor.

Whatever you make of the saying, it describes a choice most walkers do not make: a detour taken on purpose, away from the road everyone follows, to a goal that is not the famous one. The cathedral's words of welcome, in the book's translation, are for all who have come from the most diverse places to this goal of pilgrims.
For many, the cathedral's page says, Oviedo was the end of the journey, and for others the beginning of the road to Santiago. It may be both, depending on the day.
Old gestures on the road
At Arbás the bells were rung in fog, the Junta's guide says, so that pilgrims should not lose their way. Someone cared whether you arrived.
At the Cruz de la Salve, the association says, pilgrims prayed a
Salve
for protection as they looked at the mountains they would cross the next day. You do not need to pray. You can stand and look, and decide what you are asking of the day.
At La Manxoya, Asturias says, it is told that the old pilgrims cried out
¡Mi Dios!
at the first sight of the cathedral tower.
Walking with a question
You do not need a question, but if you have one it will keep you company. Here is one for each day, to take or leave.

items.t: León to La Robla.
You are leaving a city and a road you know. What are you leaving with it, and what are you carrying anyway?
La Robla to Poladura de la Tercia.
The mountain is ahead and you can see it coming. What are you afraid of, and what would you do if it happened?
Poladura de la Tercia to Pajares.
This is the day on which you may have to wait or turn back. What do you need to hear from yourself before you decide?
Pajares to Pola de Lena.
You have crossed. What can you put down now?
Pola de Lena to Mieres.
The association calls this a rest. What is it like to have nowhere to hurry to?
Mieres to Oviedo.
Tomorrow is the cathedral. Is it your goal or your starting line, and what will you do if you feel nothing at all?

spans.t: At the end

The cathedral offers pilgrims a prayer before the image of the Saviour. It asks him to be a companion to those on the roads of life, to explain the Scriptures to them, and to be known in the breaking of bread. Those words recall the walk to Emmaus in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 24. If you believe, they are yours to use. If you do not, they still describe what a long walk does: it makes you a companion to yourself, and lets you notice who else is walking beside you.
The last streets

You come in by the district of San Lázaro, and the road ends at the cathedral of San Salvador, whose Holy Chamber, Asturias says, marks the definitive end of the journey. The Junta's guide dates the cathedral to the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, and says it keeps the image of the Saviour, from the thirteenth century, which gave the road its name.

The Holy Chamber is older, and its story has changed. The cathedral says it was long believed to have been built under King Alfonso II (791 to 842), but that archaeology now points to the reign of Alfonso III (866 to 910). In October 1934 an explosion destroyed it, and it was rebuilt between 1939 and 1942.
The Sudarium

The cathedral's page on visiting says that the Sudarium always stays in the Holy Chamber, and that, for reasons of conservation, the original can be seen only three weeks a year. The rest of the time you see an exact replica. Wikipedia names Good Friday and two days in September, while the cathedral's page gives no dates, so ask which weeks it means.

The cathedral publishes a calendar of the days it opens to visitors, and some days it is closed. Look at it before you fix your arrival day. It says a full visit with its audio guide takes about an hour. It also stamps the credencial of any pilgrim who asks, whatever Camino they walk, and says a neighbouring parish church holds a pilgrims' Mass and blessing, with the time on its own page. Look there, not here.
The Salvadorana

The Salvadorana is the certificate of Oviedo's cathedral for those who have walked the road. The cathedral says it is signed by the Dean, and the association says so too. To ask for it you show a credencial stamped at the places you pass, and one stamp per stage is enough. The association adds that you can also get it at the pilgrims' hostel in Oviedo, while the cathedral's page names only the cathedral. Ask there how and when it is given.

The Confraternity of St James calls it the road's own "Compostela". That is a loose way to put it. The Compostela is a different certificate, given by a different body for a different walk, and the next section says what its rules are.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

This walk ends at Oviedo, not at Santiago. The Office's pages read for this book, on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance, do not mention the Camino del Salvador or Oviedo. So this book says nothing about whether the Office counts the kilometres you walk to Oviedo, or what it would record for them.

From Oviedo ~320 km lie ahead on the Camino Primitivo, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. If your plan is anything other than walking the Primitivo from Oviedo, or if you will walk it in stages, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go.
Onwards, if you want to

The cathedral says the Holy Chamber is the starting point of the Camino Primitivo. Opposite the statue of King Alfonso II, whom the cathedral calls the first pilgrim to Santiago, is the plaque from which the Primitivo sets out, and the branch that joins the Camino del Norte.
The Original Way
, in this series, walks the Primitivo. Your road and that one do not meet halfway: this one ends where that one begins.
The next day

Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. The cathedral is the reason you came, and it is worth seeing without a pack on your back. Plan your way home with the timetables in front of you. Oviedo has a railway station, and Asturias Airport is ~48 km away.

You walked out of a mountain and into a city, and then, quite soon, into a train or a plane. The change is sharper than on a longer road, because the road was short. Give yourself a day before you go back to the usual speed of things.

Keep your credencial, with its stamps in order, and the Salvadorana if you asked for it. Both are modest documents, and in a few years you may find they say more than a photograph. If you kept notes along the way, read them on the journey home. The questions of the inner Way are still good ones when you are no longer walking.

Some of you turned back on the third day, or took a taxi past the mountain, and wonder whether that counts. The association's answer is the one this book would give too: the Way will always be there, and you can do it another time. Walking well means knowing when the mountain says no.
If you want to keep walking, the road in front of you is already named. The Camino Primitivo begins at the cathedral where you stopped, ~320 km to Santiago, and has its own book in this series,
The Original Way
. The Camino Francés goes west from León, where you began, and has
The French Way
. Neither is a sequel that you owe. A short road can be a whole one.
Buen Camino
, in whatever direction you walk next.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app's catalog lists the Camino del Salvador as a road from León to Oviedo of ~120 km. The app is still in development, so look in it for what is available on this road today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and the fact ledger that goes with it lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: Turismo Asturias

(turismoasturias.es), the tourism service of the Principado de Asturias: the page on the Way of El Salvador, its three Asturian stages, and its practical information for pilgrims. Its English pages are machine-translated, so this book read the Spanish originals for every figure and every warning.
The Junta de Castilla y León
: its guide to the historic roads, in the chapter on the Camino del Salvador (data updated in February 2011), its leaflet map of the road, and its tourism page on the route.
The association of the Camino de San Salvador
(caminodesansalvador.org), whose members are municipalities of León province: its six stages, its plans of five to nine days, and its practical advice.
The Cabildo of the cathedral of Oviedo
(catedraldeoviedo.com): its pages on the road, the Holy Chamber, the care of pilgrims, and visiting.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino San Salvador.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.
Your Europe
, the EU's information service, for the emergency number 112, and
AEMET
, the Spanish state weather agency, for warnings and forecasts.
Wikipedia

, for history, geography and transport: its articles on León, Oviedo, the Pajares Base Tunnel and Poladura de la Tercia, and, in Spanish, on the Puerto de Pajares, the Camino de El Salvador and the confiscations of church property. The climate figures for León and Oviedo are Wikipedia's, from AEMET.
A standard solar calculation
, for sunrise and sunset at León, and
the CaminoPlus route catalog and route guide
, for the road's ends, ~120 km and difficulty rating.

spans.t: Published lengths differ, sometimes by several kilometres, and this book says so. The translations from Spanish are the author's own. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations and municipalities that mark it, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages who say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of a cathedral.
Cámara Santa
: the Holy Chamber of Oviedo's cathedral, which keeps its relics.
Collada
: a gap in a ridge.
Colegiata
: a collegiate church, as at Arbás.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Puerto
: a mountain pass.
Salvadorana
: the certificate of Oviedo's cathedral for pilgrims who have walked the road.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Sudario
: the linen cloth that tradition says covered Christ's head, kept in the Cámara Santa.
